flashcards.q: Why is DCO better framed as a bandit problem than a sequence of A/B tests?
flashcards.a: Creative performance isn't stationary -- it fatigues. A fixed-horizon A/B test can't reallocate traffic mid-test as a 'winner' starts declining; a bandit continuously shifts allocation and can pull back from a decaying arm in near-real time.

flashcards.q: Why does full-combination DCO (e.g. 4 headlines x 5 images x 3 CTAs) hit a traffic wall?
flashcards.a: 60 combinations each need roughly the per-arm sample size a single test would -- the same L^k-style cost as full-factorial MVT. Fix: feature-level/component bandits modeling each component's marginal contribution instead of each full combination.

flashcards.q: What assumption do component-level (feature-level) DCO bandits make, and when does it fail?
flashcards.a: They assume components combine roughly additively (limited interaction effects) -- the same bet fractional-factorial designs make. Fails when a specific pairing (e.g. one headline with one image) has a real interaction the additive model can't capture; that pairing should be tested as its own arm.

flashcards.q: Define creative fatigue and its common heuristic thresholds.
flashcards.a: Decline in engagement (CTR, hook rate) as the same audience sees a creative repeatedly. Heuristic flags: CTR decline ~10%+, CPA rise ~15%+, frequency exceeding ~3 impressions/user in prospecting campaigns -- category/context-dependent, not universal constants.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a plain bandit automatically handle creative fatigue?
flashcards.a: A standard bandit's reward estimate is an un-decayed average/posterior over all history, implicitly assuming stationary reward. It keeps believing a fatiguing creative is as good as its historical average for a while after true performance starts declining, over-allocating traffic to it.

flashcards.q: Name two fixes for fatigue-unaware bandits.
flashcards.a: Exponential decay / sliding window on the reward estimate (weights recent observations more, tracks decline), and explicit per-user frequency capping (hard limit independent of the reward signal, addressing the frequency-driven fatigue mechanism directly).

flashcards.q: Reactive vs proactive fatigue detection -- what's the difference and why does the gap matter?
flashcards.a: Reactive fires once an aggregate metric (CTR/CPA) crosses a threshold, by definition after meaningful decline already happened. Proactive uses early engagement-curve shape to predict decay before the aggregate metric visibly crosses a threshold, catching fatigue earlier and reducing wasted spend.

flashcards.q: What reported real-world magnitudes exist for bandit-based creative allocation vs static rotation?
flashcards.a: Thompson Sampling: ~8% customer acquisition lift at no added cost (retail banking display case study). Bandit-based selection: ~10% CTR lift vs static baseline (online retail case study). Context-specific, not universal guarantees.

flashcards.q: How does frequency capping interact with a bandit's exploration logic, and why isn't reward decay a substitute for it?
flashcards.a: Frequency capping is a hard per-user constraint applied independently of reward-driven allocation, removing an arm from eligibility for that user once hit. Decay handles population-level average fatigue over time but doesn't guarantee any single user avoids excessive repeat exposure -- the two mechanisms are complementary, not substitutes.

flashcards.q: What creative-specific bug commonly causes sample ratio mismatch in creative tests?
flashcards.a: A broken image asset or truncated headline that fails to render on a specific device/browser combination for one variant, silently dropping impressions/clicks from that variant in a way that isn't randomly distributed across the audience.

flashcards.q: Why is Thompson Sampling generally a better default than UCB for a fast-moving, fatigue-prone creative portfolio?
flashcards.a: UCB's confidence bounds typically assume stationary rewards and stay tight (slow to react) as an arm accumulates observations even as true performance declines. Thompson Sampling's posterior naturally re-widens when combined with decayed/windowed observations, fitting the non-stationary fatigue pattern better.

flashcards.q: When is UCB still a reasonable choice over Thompson Sampling for ad creative allocation?
flashcards.a: When the portfolio refreshes frequently enough that non-stationarity isn't dominant, or when deterministic, easier-to-audit allocation behavior matters for stakeholder-facing reporting â€” the choice trades non-stationarity handling against auditability/simplicity, not a universal ranking.
